title: Card transactions with fraud flags, September 2026

findings.headline: Night-time transactions have a very high fraud rate
findings.detail: Fraud is flagged on 30.8% of the 718 transactions made between midnight and 5am, against 0.3% to 0.7% in other periods. Night is only 7% of volume.

findings.headline: Fraud rate rose sharply in mid-September
findings.detail: The weekly fraud rate went from 0.6% (week of 31 Aug) to 4.0% (14 Sep) and 4.1% (21 Sep), before easing to 1.8% in the last week. The last week is partial, with 727 rows, so treat it with care.

findings.headline: Digital goods, online and AE/SG are concentrated risk pockets
findings.detail: Fraud is 20.4% in Digital goods, 6.3% online, 28.6% in AE (206 rows) and 31.0% in SG (187 rows). Other categories are at 0.7% or below, and contactless and chip are at 0.5% or below. These patterns may overlap, so they may not be separate problems.

findings.headline: Small-value transactions are far more likely to be fraud
findings.detail: The lowest amount band (1.71 to 535.9, 2,052 rows) has an 11.4% fraud rate. The four higher bands range from 0.3% to 0.6%, which suggests small test-style purchases deserve a look.

findings.headline: Data is complete, and the main market looks calm
findings.detail: There are no missing cells or duplicate rows across 10,260 transactions. India is 93.5% of rows with a 1.6% fraud rate, and the overall rate is 2.7% (272 cases).

next_steps: Check whether the night, online, digital goods, AE/SG and low-value fraud cases are the same transactions, using a cross-tab of those flags.
Review the 272 fraud cases from the weeks of 14 and 21 September to see what changed, such as merchants, cards or channels.
Test tighter rules or step-up checks for night-time online digital goods and AE/SG purchases, and measure the effect on genuine customers.

conclusion: The data is complete and shows fraud is heavily concentrated: at night, in Digital goods, online, in AE and SG, in low-value purchases, and in the weeks of 14 and 21 September. These groups probably overlap, so treat them as one pattern until shown otherwise. First, cross-tabulate these flags to find the smallest set of transactions that holds most of the 272 cases.
limits: This review uses summary figures only, so it cannot show how the groups overlap, what changed in September, or why any pattern exists.
